summary: The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending business, and the assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer added a sum of money of Rs.1,50,00,000 estimatedas the accrued interest, on the assessee "s account in the books of account of the assessee on the valuation date". The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that the Wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee the interest due on accrual basis as it was not realised on the outstandings of the money lending business. The Appellate Tribunal held that the Wealth tax Officer was in fact justified in including the interest due to the assessee in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The High Court in appeal held that the wealth tax Officer was not in law justified under the provisions of section 27(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1961, and that the Wealthtax Officer was in error in excluding the interest due from the assessee on accrual basis. The High court, in appeal, held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Wealth tax Act, 1964, and that, in any event, the interest due under the Wealth Tax Acts was not includible in the wealth of the assesse. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. The Wealth tax Officer is not in law entitled to deduct the interest due as a result of the valuation of the assets of the assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, from the assets of an assessee under the Wealth tax Acts. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the WealthTax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuationdate. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When the asset is a asset other than the cash, its market value is determined by the valuation date. [310E F] 2. The expression "net wealth" is defined by section 2(m) of the Act as "the value of any asset which is the subject of the wealth tax law". The expression 'net wealth ' is defined by clause (m) of section 2(n) of the Income Tax Act, as "the valuation date". It is not the same thing as the valuation date, and the expression "net Wealth" is defined as "the date of the valuation". The expression is defined in section 2(o) of the Indian Income Tax Act as "a valuation date". [310F G] 3. The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff, filed a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property in question. The defendants, however, contended that the suit was barred by res judicata and/or constructive res judicata as found in the plaint. The Trial Court dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the suit had been barred by resjudicata. The High court, however, found that the suit filed by the appellants was barred by constructive res judicata and the High Court, therefore, dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was barred under section 58(2) of the Act. [1030F] 1.2 The suit was not maintainable and deserved to be dismissed. [1031F] 1:3 The suit was filed by the legal representatives on the basis of the pleadings in the suit and the nature of the questions required to be determined for grant or refusal of relief claimed in the suit. [1032G] 1.3 The suit filed by a co plaintiff for declaration and injunction was not maintainable. [1033G] 1:4 The suit was maintainable and deserved by the plaintiff for the relief claimed in it. [1034G] 1 :4 The suit is not maintainable and deserve to be dismissed under section 58 (2) of Act. [1045G] 1 2. The suit is barred by res Judicata. [1035G] 2. [1036B] 2.1 The relief claimed is for a declaratory relief and the suit must be filed within one year from the date of the suit. It is not necessary that the relief should be filed within the period of limitation. [1037C] 2.2 The relief claimed by the plaintiff is for a decree for a declaration, and consequential relief, and the suit should be filed in the Court of the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Court if the issue is held against the defendant. [1038D] 3. The suit filed in the present case was not maintainable as the suit was filed within one years from the date on which the suit was instituted. [1039D] 4. The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunathayam of Manjakollai village in the State of Madras. The appellant was elected to the office of the President of the Sama tha Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras. The respondents challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant was a Mahant of a temple and was not a hereditary trustee. The appellant is a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The appellant had a hereditary trustee as a trustee and the appeal was not barred under section 6( 9) of the Act. [426 C] (2) The appellant is not a hereditary trustees within the meaning ofs.6(9) and the suit is not barred by the Act. The appellant cannot succeed to his own office. [426 D] (3) The appellant cannot be allowed to raise a contention that the office of a trustee in the temple of the Kumaran Koil is not hereditary. The appellant could not succeed to his office as a matter of right. [426 E] (4) The appellant had no hereditary office of hereditary trustee in the Temple of the Kumarans of the Kumara Hindu Religious and Religious Endowments, Madras, and the suit filed by the appellant was not barred. [426 F] (5) The appellant could succeed to his place of residence and the office of his successor was not hereditary. [426 A] (6) The office of the appellant is hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(1) of the Bombay Act 19 of1951. The appellant, therefore, was a hereditary Mahant within the meaningof section 6(8) of the Tamil Nadu Act 19 of 1961. [426 B]

The appellant company was a company engaged in the manufacture of cement. The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, claimed that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to award bonus to the workmen of the company. The Tribunal held that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that there was no identical industry in the region in which minimum wage was fixed. The Tribunal also held that the award of the Tribunal was not binding on the parties. The Tribunal, however, held that there was a difference between the two groups of workmen in the region and that the Tribunal should have awarded bonus on the basis of the consolidated wages. The Tribunal further held that the company was not entitled to the bonus claimed. The Tribunal accordingly held that the Company was entitled to bonus on the same basis as the permanent workers. The Tribunal however, held in favour of the workmen. The Tribunal found that the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction to award the bonus on the ground that the Tribunal failed to determine the minimum wage. The Tribunal therefore, allowed the appeal to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the Tribunal erred in holding that no identical industry was in the region. The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and at the time of reference, the Tribunal was expected, to decide the matter only as referred. [689F] The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in holding that it was not correct to say that the Tribunal committed any error of law. [680F] The award of the Industrial Tribunal was set aside. The Tribunal had to decide the question whether the Tribunal was right or whether it was right in the view that the Tribunal ought to have awarded bonus. [681F] The question whether the tribunal was right in awarding bonus on the principle of industry cum region was a matter for the Tribunal to decide. [682F] The fact that the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the disputes is not a matter for determination by the Tribunal. The Tribunal has to decide the questions referred to it. [683F] The present case is not one of the same nature. The Tribunal should have decided the dispute only in the light of the observations of this Court in the case of Indian Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs Workmen, [1963] 1 S.C.R. 933. In the present case, the Tribunal had to determine the question whether there was a distinction between the two sets of workmen in that region and the question whether it was a consolidated wage consisting of the two elements of basic wage and dearness allowance. The Tribunal did not decide the question. [685F]

The respondents, who were the owners of the coal mines, filed a suit for the recovery of the possession of the lands and for a declaration that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines and that the respondents were entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The respondents contended that the respondents could not be entitled to any damages. The respondents denied that they had encroached upon the coal mines and claimed that the respondents ' claim was barred by limitation. The respondents pleaded that the respondents having failed to establish that the respondents came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of the coal removed beyond three years prior to the suit, the respondents had no right to claim any damages. Held, that the respondents did not have knowledge of the removal and the respondents had knowledge of the appellant 's encroachment of their coal mines only in the year 1941 which was within three years of the date of the filing of the suit. The respondents had knowledge that the appellant had encroached upon any portion of their coal mine. The respondents could not claim any damages for the period of the suit and the appellant could not claim damages for the said period. The respondents were not entitled to any compensation for the period during which they had been wrongfully evicted. The respondents did not claim any compensation for their unauthorised occupation of the coal mine. Held, further, that the finding of the courts below that the respondents have knowledge of a fact is not a finding of fact. The respondents have knowledge that the respondents' possession of the mines was not lost to them by being rendered unworkable. The respondents, therefore, had knowledge of their illegal encroachment of their land mines only in 1952 which was within the four years of the filing.

The appellant was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on the appellant. The appellant challenged the order of the tribunal on the ground that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing orders. The appellant contended that the tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass an order of dismissal and that the order was not a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by r. 18 (a) of Standing orders. Held, that the tribunal was not competent to pass an award under r.18(a) and the order was therefore a bona fide order. The appellant could not rest its case merely on r. 18. The appellant cannot rest its case on the ground of mala fides. The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication. The tribunal was of the view that the exercise of power was colourable and it could not be said that the action taken under r, 18(a), was a colourable exercise of power and was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The appellant did not satisfy the tribunal that the exercise was bona fide and was not bonafide. The appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed. The appellant had not been given an opportunity to show what had actually happened. The appellant therefore could not rest his case merely on a rule of natural justice. The appellant, therefore, cannot rest its claim merely on r, 18 (a).

The appellant, a member of a Scheduled Caste, was elected as a member of the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constituency. The appellant challenged the election on various grounds. The Election Tribunal rejected the appellant 's contention that the appellant did not belong to a Scheduled Caste. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. The appellant contended that the appellant belonged to a Scheduled Tribe and that the appellant was not a member of any Scheduled Caste. Held, that the appellant belongs to a Scheduled caste and was entitled to be declared elected. The appellant was a member of Scheduled Caste and was entitled only to be declared as a member. The appellant did not fall within the definition of a Scheduled Tribe. The appellant had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group of Sahas. The appellant could not be declared elected as a Member of the Scheduled Caste. He must be held to belong to a larger caste group of Sunris. The appellant must be held by the larger caste group. The appellant, a company, entered into an agreement with the respondents, entered into a contract with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure, prescribed by the award, and the respondents, an award, had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an award, and, in pursuance of that award, the appellant paid the wages authority, the respondents, the said prescribed wages, the said minimum wages, the rate of wages fixed by the award. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents, that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the Act, and that the respondents had no right to claim the benefit of section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended that the appellant was not entitled to claim the benefits of the Act as the wages fixed by it did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) of the Act and that the appellant had no right, under section 15 of that Act, to claim the same. The appellant, a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore, was carrying on business in the erstwhile State of Travancore. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax on the ground that the income of the appellant was not liable to tax. The Incometax Officer rejected the assessee 's appeal and held that the banking business of the appellant being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State for the purposes of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court of Travancore Cochin held that the Banking business of the assessee being one and composite for the purpose Of the Indian Income Tax Act, the assessee was entitled to deduction of the losses incurred in the Travancore State and under section 10 of the Indian Act the assessee was not entitled to deduct income tax for that year. The High court in appeal held that the assessee was a public limited Company and that the assessee could not be said to be a public limited limited company and that the income tax was payable by the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the assessee was liable to be taxed in the Indian Income ' tax Act, 1922, was not answered by the High Court. The assessee was a private limited company and was carrying on the business in the Travancore States. The assessee had a public limited business in the State and it was carrying on its business in the other States. The business in the two territories was one and indivisible and the assessee was carrying on his business in the latter State. The assessee could not therefore be said to have been a public limited companies. [260 E F] (ii) The assessee was not a public limitedcompany and was not liable for the loss of profits or gains arising out of the business in an Indian State. The income tax was not payable by the appellant. The income of the assessee was therefore not liable to be included in the income of his business in an Income tax Act, and the income tax could not be deducted. [260 F G] (iii) The assessee 's contention that the banking company was not liable under section 10(2) (e) and (2) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1923, was not correct. The assessee ' was a public company and was not a private limited Company. The income was not liable. The income, therefore, was not liable, to be included under section 10. [260 G H] (iv) The assessee could only be said to represent the profits of the business of the company in the Travancore. State and not the profits of its business in an 'other State ' or so divide business. The income taxed was not liable in the Indian State but was liable to tax under the Indian Income. tax Act, 1918. The income which was liable to income tax was liable to the assessee. The income could not be included in its income in the Indian Indian State. [260 H] (v) The assessee had no business in the Malabar State and was not entitled for deduction of the loss incurred outside Travancore.

It was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition and that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the age of compulsory retirement should be fixed at 60. The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The respondent entered into a contract with the appellants for a period from 1st April, 1952, to 30 8 1953, and the appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. The appellants filed a suit for a declaration that the lease granted by them was invalid and for a declaration of their rights and for a permanent injunction restraining the respondent from interfering with their possession. The suit was dismissed by the trial court. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing the notice under section 12 of the , and that the notice was not valid. The High 'Court, however, held that the notice in question was not valid and that the respondent had no authority to go back upon his own contracts. The High. Court also held that the appellants had no authority under the Act to go back on their own contracts. Held, that the respondent could not be said to have been acting within his powers in issuing the notices under section 12. The section expressly authorised the custodian to vary the terms of the lease, and the respondent could be said to act within his authority. The section was intended to be read as a whole and the respondent was exercising his authority in the form of a notice to sell the mills and factory to the appellants. The section did not confer any authority on the custodian to cancel the lease in favour of the appellants. It was not necessary for the respondent to go back to his own contracts and to send daily reports to the Custodian of the transactions with reference thereto. The section clearly intended to repel a possible contention that section 12 did not confer upon the custodian any authority the power to cancel the agreement to sell the mill and the factory to the appellant. The section further provided that the custodian could cancel the agreement if he was satisfied that the agreement was not valid, and that the agreement could be cancelled by the custodian. The section thus did not confer on the custodian any power to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof. The section merely intended to repress the parties from the operation of the section. The section does not confer any power on the custodian or the custodian to revoke the lease in his favour. The section, therefore, did not confer an authority on the Custodian to cancel the contract in favour of a third party. The section therefore did not confer a power on the Custodian in issuing the notification under section 12 to cancel the deed of lease in favour Of the appellants.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on an ad hoc basis. He was confirmed in the post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an adhoc basis. The appellant was confirmed in his post in course. On January 25, 1974. the appellant was promoted as Head Clerk on a regular basis. On April 1, 1975, the appellant was confirmed as a Head Clerks. The appellant, who was the lessee of a minor mineral, applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah of Venkatagiri, and the Collector, on the same day, granted a lease for a period of 20 years to the appellant. The appellant contended that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of the Act and that the lease could not be terminated by the Government without any compensation. The Collector held that the lease granted to the appellant was not a mining lease within the definition of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant then appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the lease in question was a lease within section 20(1) of the Act, and the lease was a lease for the period of 20,000 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. The appellant was not entitled to the renewal of the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules of 1949. The appellant had not been given a notice of the renewal of his lease and the appellant was entitled to the grant of the lease for a further period of 20. The appellant could not be allowed to claim the renewal of its lease under r, 47 of the Act as the lease was determined under the second proviso to section 20(i) of the Abolition Act. The second proviso to r. 47 was enacted to nullify the creation of rights after July 1, 1945, even if that rule had the effect of modifying the terms of the lease itself. The appellant 's case was that the lease had been determined under the first proviso to r, 47, and the second proviso was not a contract of lease. The appellant did not claim the renewal as the lease had expired on November 30. 1947. In the present case, the lease was terminated on November 30 and November 30, 1950. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for the renewal of a lease under r 47 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948. The appellant must be held to have been given a fresh lease for a term exceeding the duration of the original lease. 48 of the Mineral Rules of 1948, which was enacted to validate the lease, was not a statutory provision and the appellant could not claim the benefit of the second proviso. The appellant cannot be allowed to contend that the second proviso did not apply to the rights created after July 1. 1945. The appellant should have been given an opportunity of being heard before the expiry of the lease and the second Proviso to the second proviso could not be invoked.
